c.tagline: Japan's best-preserved castle town — a legendary garden, gold leaf, and geisha teahouse streets.

taxi.fareNote: Ride-hailing apps (GO, Uber) only dispatch licensed metered taxis rather than private cars, and coverage is thinner than in Tokyo or Osaka — flagging a metered taxi at a rank or by phone is often quickest. The Kanazawa Loop Bus covers most sightseeing.

avoid.reason: Katamachi's nightlife strip has occasional bar touts late at night; otherwise just usual awareness.

hood_desc: The transport hub around JR Kanazawa Station and its dramatic wooden Tsuzumi Gate, where the Hokuriku Shinkansen from Tokyo arrives; ringed by hotels, department stores and the Loop Bus terminal. The most convenient base for first-timers who want maximum connectivity.

Kanazawa's main downtown for shopping, dining and nightlife — Korinbo's department stores flow into Katamachi's dense grid of izakaya, bars and clubs along the Sai River. Walkable to Omicho Market, the 21st Century Museum and Kenroku-en, and the go-to area for going out.

The largest and most atmospheric of Kanazawa's three geisha teahouse districts, a preserved lattice-fronted quarter of wooden chaya, gold-leaf shops, tea salons and traditional ryokan. The most beautiful, culture-steeped place to stay in old Japan.

The historic and cultural core around Kanazawa Castle Park and Kenroku-en, one of Japan's three great gardens, alongside the 21st Century Museum of Contemporary Art and Oyama Shrine. Ideal for sightseeing at a calm, green pace.

water.note: Tap water is safe and good quality.

transit.pay: Tap a nationwide Suica/ICOCA IC card or the local ICa card, or pay cash on board; a flat city-bus fare is around ¥200 (~$1.35). A one-day Loop Bus / city-bus pass (about ¥600) covers most sightseeing and is the best value for a day of touring.
transit.hours: Loop and city buses run roughly 8:00am to 6:00pm (a limited Light-Up Bus adds evening runs to key sights); after the buses stop, taxis fill the gap.
transit.note: Kanazawa has no subway or tram — the clockwise/counter-clockwise Kanazawa Loop Bus and the wider Hokutetsu bus network are the main way to reach the sights, and the compact center is very walkable.

bus: Highway buses to Tokyo, Nagoya, Osaka & Kyoto

transit.m: Hokutetsu limousine bus to Kanazawa Station West Gate (~40-45 min, hourly)
Airport shuttle bus to JR Komatsu Station, then IR Ishikawa Line or Shinkansen to Kanazawa

tip.r: Not customary; tipping is not expected anywhere in Japan and can cause confusion.

food.name: Kaisendon at Omicho Market
food.desc: Rice bowl heaped with Sea of Japan seafood - snow crab, sweet shrimp, yellowtail and salmon roe - cut to order in a 300-year-old market.

places.name: Yamasan Sushi
places.note: Veteran market sushi counter known for generously piled seafood bowls.

places.name: Mori Mori Sushi Omicho
places.note: Popular conveyor-style sushi using local Ishikawa catch; expect a wait at lunch.

places.name: Omicho Ichiba-kan food floor
places.note: Upper-floor eateries with kaisendon and grilled fish; easier to get a seat.

food.name: Jibuni
food.desc: Kanazawa's signature stew: flour-dusted duck simmered in sweet dashi with sudare-fu wheat gluten and vegetables, finished with sharp wasabi.

places.name: Tsubajin
places.note: Historic Kaga cuisine restaurant dating to the 18th century; classic jibuni course.

places.name: Miyoshian
places.note: Teahouse restaurant beside the garden pond serving jibuni set lunches.

places.name: Kagaya
places.note: Long-standing traditional restaurant preserving Kanazawa recipes.

food.name: Kanazawa oden
food.desc: Year-round oden in a pale, delicate dashi with local extras like kuruma-fu wheat gluten, baigai sea snails and crab-roe koubako in winter.

places.name: Akadama Honten
places.note: Kanazawa oden institution running since the 1920s; the benchmark bowl in town.

places.name: Kuroyuri
places.note: Convenient station oden counter with local ingredients and Ishikawa sake.

places.name: Oden Takasago
places.note: Small old-school counter shop popular with locals for winter crab oden.

food.name: Gold-leaf soft-serve ice cream
food.desc: Vanilla soft-serve wrapped in a full sheet of edible gold leaf; Kanazawa produces almost all of Japan's gold leaf, so this is a local joke turned icon.

places.name: Hakuichi Higashiyama
places.note: The shop that made gold-leaf soft-serve famous; also sells gold-leaf crafts.

places.name: Hakuza Higashiyama
places.note: Gold-leaf specialist with a gold-walled tearoom and gold-flecked sweets.

places.name: Kanakan Joy
places.note: Market stand doing gold-leaf ice cream between the seafood counters.

food.name: Nodoguro and buri (grilled local fish)
food.desc: Blackthroat seaperch grilled with salt, and winter buri yellowtail simmered with daikon - the two fish Ishikawa people rate above all others.

places.name: Itaru Honten
places.note: Famous izakaya for Ishikawa seafood and sake; book well ahead.

places.name: Omicho Market food stalls
places.note: Grill counters cook nodoguro and buri to order at market prices.

places.name: Fuwari
places.note: Izakaya focused on Noto seafood and Kaga vegetables with a strong sake list.

food.name: Kaburazushi
food.desc: Winter delicacy of salted turnip layered with yellowtail and fermented in sweet rice koji - pungent, funky and unique to the Hokuriku coast.

places.name: Omicho Market pickle shops
places.note: Several stalls sell kaburazushi in winter, vacuum-packed for travel.

places.name: Itaru Honten
places.note: Serves kaburazushi in season as an appetiser with local sake.

places.name: Fuwari
places.note: Regional fermented specialities appear on the seasonal menu.

food.name: Ishikawa sake
food.desc: Hokuriku rice and soft water make clean, food-friendly sake; look for Kanazawa's Fukumitsuya and nearby Tedorigawa and Kagatobi breweries.

places.name: Fukumitsuya Sake Shop
places.note: Kanazawa's oldest brewery, founded 1625; tasting and shop on site.

places.name: Itaru Honten
places.note: Deep Ishikawa sake list matched to seafood; the classic pairing venue.

places.name: Kuroyuri
places.note: Easy station stop for local sake flights with oden.

food.name: Kaga bocha roasted tea
food.desc: Kanazawa's own tea, roasted from tea stems rather than leaves, giving a toasty, low-caffeine cup served in teahouses and after Kaga meals.

places.name: Kaikaro
places.note: Restored geisha teahouse open to visitors; tea served in gilded rooms.

places.name: Miyoshian
places.note: Tea and sweets overlooking Kasumigaike pond in the famous garden.

places.name: Hakuichi Higashiyama
places.note: Cafe counter pairing bocha with gold-leaf sweets.

landmarks: Kenroku-en Garden
One of Japan's three most celebrated landscape gardens, perfecting six classical attributes across ponds, teahouses and the iconic two-legged Kotoji stone lantern.
Kanazawa Castle Park
The Maeda clan's partly reconstructed castle showcases dazzling white lead-tiled roofs, massive gates and masterful joinery beside Kenroku-en.
Higashi Chaya District
Kanazawa's largest geisha quarter preserves wooden teahouses with slatted kimusuko facades, gold-leaf boutiques and the chance to hear a shamisen drift at dusk.
21st Century Museum of Contemporary Art
A glass-walled circular museum famous for Leandro Erlich's illusionary Swimming Pool, blurring art and play in the city center.
Ōmichō Market
For nearly 300 years Kanazawa's kitchen, its 170 stalls pile snow crab, sweet shrimp and glistening kaisendon seafood bowls each morning.
Nagamachi Samurai District and Nomura-ke Residence
Earthen-walled lanes and canals lead to the restored Nomura samurai house, whose tiny garden is ranked among Japan's finest.
Myōryū-ji (Ninja Temple)
This deceptive 1643 temple conceals trapdoors, hidden staircases and secret rooms built to defend the Maeda lords from shogunate spies.
Oyama Shrine
A shrine to Lord Maeda Toshiie whose unusual three-story gate blends Japanese, Chinese and Dutch styles, crowned with stained glass once used as a lighthouse.
D.T. Suzuki Museum
A minimalist masterpiece of still water and empty space honoring the philosopher who introduced Zen to the West, inviting quiet contemplation.
Kazue-machi Chaya District
A slender riverside geisha quarter along the Asano River, its lantern-lit teahouses reflected in the water on atmospheric evening strolls.

train.note: Japan has no international trains. The Hokuriku Shinkansen links Kanazawa to Tokyo in about 2 hours 30 minutes and, since the March 2024 extension, runs south to Tsuruga where you change for Kyoto and Osaka - the old through Thunderbird express from Osaka now terminates at Tsuruga, so allow for that connection. IR Ishikawa Railway and JR conventional lines cover the wider Hokuriku region, including Wakura Onsen on the Noto Peninsula. Reserved Shinkansen seats open 1 month ahead and fill fast in cherry-blossom season.

bus.note: No international buses serve Japan. Long-distance and overnight highway buses leave the Kanazawa Station east-gate terminal for Tokyo, Nagoya, Kyoto, Osaka and Takayama - the main operators are Hokutetsu, Willer Express (https://willerexpress.com/en/) and the JR bus group. Takayama is about 2 hours 15 minutes by coach and has no direct train, so the bus is the only sensible link. Willer sells online in English; Hokutetsu seats are usually bought at the terminal counter.

ferry.note: Kanazawa Port handles cargo and occasional cruise ships rather than scheduled passenger ferries, so there are no regular boat services for travellers. The nearest useful sailings are from Niigata or Tsuruga on the Sea of Japan coast, both several hours away.

half.name: Kaga Onsen
half.blurb: A cluster of historic hot-spring resort towns (Yamashiro, Yamanaka, Katayamazu) about 40 minutes south by train, good for a soak and riverside walks.

half.name: Natadera Temple
half.blurb: An atmospheric 1,300-year-old Buddhist temple set among carved rock caves and gardens near Komatsu.

half.name: Noto Peninsula (Wakura)
half.blurb: Rugged Sea-of-Japan coastline and the Wakura Onsen hot springs on the peninsula north of the city.

full.name: Shirakawa-go
full.blurb: A UNESCO village of steep thatched gassho-zukuri farmhouses in the mountains, about 1h15 by express bus.

full.name: Takayama
full.blurb: A beautifully preserved Edo-era old town in the Hida mountains, reachable by bus via Shirakawa-go.

full.name: Eiheiji Temple
full.blurb: A vast, active Zen Buddhist training monastery of moss and cedar in the mountains of neighboring Fukui.
